attributes.body_ja:
「上（うえ）で」は、「(A) をしてから」や「(A) をした後（あと）で」を意味（いみ）する表現（ひょうげん）です。動詞（どうし）の過去形（かこけい）や「の」が付（つ）いた名詞（めいし）のあとで使（つか）われます。この文法（ぶんぽう）は、名詞（めいし）の「上」と格助詞（かくじょし）の「で」からできていて、「まず (A) をして、そのあとに (B) をする」という流（なが）れを表（あらわ）すときに使（つか）われます。

「上（うえ）で」は、かたい表現（ひょうげん）なので、日常（にちじょう）のくだけた会話（かいわ）ではあまり使（つか）われません。(A) が (B) のための条件（じょうけん）であるときや、(A) のあとに (B) をするのが自然（しぜん）であるときによく使（つか）われます。

注意点（ちゅういてん）

「上（うえ）で」の文（ぶん）の (A) と (B) には、自分（じぶん）の意思（いし）で行（おこな）う行動（こうどう）が入（はい）ります。また、「上（うえ）で」を使（つか）うときは、(A) に受（う）け身（み）の動詞（どうし）を使（つか）うことはできません。日本語（にほんご）の受（う）け身（み）は、その動作（どうさ）を自分（じぶん）の意思（いし）では変（か）えられないことを表（あらわ）すことが多（おお）いためです。
attributes.body:
上（うえ）で is an expression in Japanese that is used after the past form of verbs, or nouns followed by の. It shows that something will happen 'after (A)', or 'upon (A)'. This grammar point is used in a similar way to its literal meaning, which is 'with the above/previous (A), (B)'. 上（うえ） as 'above', and で as 'with', in で's use as a case marking particle.

上（うえ）で is a structure that is primarily used in formal settings. Due to this, it will not be used in casual conversations very often. It also strongly hints at (A) being a requirement for (B), or (A) being something that would logically be expected before (B).

Caution

Due to 上（うえ）で being used to show logical progressions from (A) to (B), (A) cannot be a verb that is passive. Passivity in Japanese often implies that someone/thing has a lack of control in relation to the actions that happen to them/it. As a result of this, (A) not being able to be controlled would result in (B) sounding like it could not be planned for.

This is different to the way that passivity works in English (simply showing that something received an action upon it).

attributes.source: A Dictionary of Intermediate Japanese Grammar

attributes.description: What is the difference between 上で and 後で?
Excellent breakdown of sentences with うえで

attributes.body: Both 上で and あとで express that one action follows another, but with different nuances. あとで simply shows sequence, like 'after doing (A)'. 上で implies the first action is a necessary step for the second, similar to 'upon doing (A)', and is more formal, often used in writing or business contexts.

Both can express the idea of 'after doing (A), (B)', but 上で focuses on process or sequence (lit. 'upon' doing), e.g. 話し合った上で決めましょう ('Let's decide after discussing it.'). In contrast, た末・の末 emphasizes an outcome after prolonged effort or struggle, e.g. 悩んだ末に転職した ('After much deliberation, I changed jobs.').

Both show one action leading to another, but with different focus. て初めて marks a first experience or realization, e.g. 大人になって初めて分かった ('I only understood after becoming an adult.') 上で shows a necessary step before the next action, e.g. 社長に相談した上で決めましょう ('Let's decide after consulting the president.')

first_relatable.title: て初めて
first_relatable.meaning: For the first time, Not until, Only after, Only when, Only because

attributes.body: Both use 上 but differ quite a bit in meaning. 上に adds information, like '(B) in addition to (or 'on top of') (A)', typically within the same general category, e.g. 彼は親切な上に頭もいい ('He's smart in addition to being kind.'). In contrast, 上で expresses an action happening after (lit. 'upon') another action or condition being realized, e.g. 社長に相談した上で決めましょう ('Let's decide after consulting the president.').

first_relatable.title: 上に
first_relatable.meaning: As well, Besides, In addition to

attributes.body: Both 上で and たら can describe sequences or conditions, but with different nuance. 上で implies that one action is a prerequisite for another, such as 社長と相談した上で決めましょう ('Let's decide after discussing it with the president.'). たら is more general and covers a wider range of temporal and conditional uses, as in 晴れたら散歩に行こう ('If it's sunny, let's go for a walk.').

second_relatable.title: たら
second_relatable.meaning: When, From when, Just when, If

attributes.body: てから and 上で both convey a sequence of events, but their nuances differ. てから simply indicates that one event follows another. In contrast, 上で emphasizes that the first action or event was a necessary precondition for the second event. Also, 上で is more formal than てから, and often used in business situations or writing.
